summaries.example: Imagine a club selling a “science” kit that promises better grades. The club makes a fancy chart and holds a meeting, but it never lets other people repeat the test. When students report no improvement, the club says the test was done incorrectly. This may look like science, but it avoids fair checking and protects its claim from evidence.
summaries.summary: The entry asks how we can tell science from pseudoscience. Science is a group of fact-finding practices that try to gain reliable knowledge through testing, criticism, and improvement. Pseudoscience is different from simply making a mistake or studying a non-scientific subject. It usually involves an unusual claim or teaching that is not supported by good science and is presented as scientific or as the best knowledge about its subject. Some supporters copy the appearance of science with special groups, meetings, or publications. Others try to make people doubt well-supported science. Philosophers have suggested many tests, such as whether a claim can be proved wrong, solves research problems, makes progress, or follows good rules for sharing and checking knowledge. No single test works perfectly in every case. Even so, recognizing false science is important because poor information can affect health, public decisions, news, education, and legal judgments.
key_ideas: Not everything that is not science is pseudoscience. Some activities are simply outside science, while others are poor attempts at science.
Pseudoscience often copies the outside look of science, such as making journals, conferences, or charts, without following science’s quality rules.
Good science stays open to criticism and changes when strong evidence shows that an idea is wrong.
It matters to tell science from false science when people must make choices about health, the environment, schools, news, or courts.
Experts may disagree about one perfect definition, but they often agree about many particular examples.
summaries.why_it_matters: People use information to make choices. If a false claim is dressed up as science, people may trust an ineffective treatment, misunderstand an environmental danger, or be misled by news. Learning to ask how evidence was gathered, whether others can check it, and whether criticism is taken seriously helps us become careful thinkers without treating every mistake as dishonest pseudoscience.

important_terms.definition: Careful ways of finding out how things are, using evidence, testing, and criticism.
A claim or practice that is not good science but tries to look like science or act as the most reliable source of knowledge.
Information or evidence that shows a belief may be wrong.
A way of finding out whether a claim works by checking it fairly, often more than once.

questions_to_think_about: Does a claim allow other people to check it?
What happens when evidence disagrees with the claim?
Can a mistake be ordinary bad science rather than pseudoscience?
Why might someone want a claim to look scientific?

summaries.example: Consider two researchers who make a mistake in a laboratory. One accepts colleagues’ criticism and corrects the result. The other repeatedly publishes weak experiments to defend one unorthodox theory, ignores conflicting findings, and presents the theory as reliable science. The first case is bad science; the second better illustrates pseudoscience because it combines poor support with a continuing doctrine and resistance to criticism.
summaries.summary: The entry treats pseudoscience as part of a larger philosophical question: which beliefs are epistemically warranted, or supported well enough to count as reliable knowledge? A simple boundary between science and everything else is misleading. Non-scientific subjects, ordinary mistakes, and poor research are not automatically pseudoscience. A common account requires both a lack of scientific quality and an attempt to create the impression of science. A wider account includes doctrines presented as the most reliable knowledge even when they do not explicitly call themselves scientific. The entry surveys competing criteria. Verification approaches focus on possible confirmation; Popper’s falsificationism focuses on possible conflict with observation; Kuhn stresses normal science’s puzzle-solving; Lakatos examines progressive research programmes; and other views emphasize scientific norms, integration, or systematicity. Because each single criterion has problems, many philosophers use multiple criteria or a broader assessment. There is substantial agreement about many cases, despite continuing disagreement about the best general test.
key_ideas: Pseudoscience is not identical with non-science or with every instance of unscientific work. It commonly includes a deviant doctrine and an effort to present it as scientific or as the most reliable knowledge.
The word pseudoscience is value-laden: it is used critically, not as a neutral label. This makes a purely descriptive definition difficult.
Popper emphasized falsifiability, while Kuhn emphasized the puzzle-solving work of normal science. Lakatos instead assessed whether whole research programmes make scientific progress.
Multicriterial approaches use several warning signs, including unwillingness to test, selective evidence, unrepeatable experiments, and methods that can confirm a claim but never disconfirm it.
Science denial often manufactures the appearance of a scientific controversy where there is broad agreement, whereas pseudo-theory promotion mainly advances an alternative theory.
The boundary is partly time-dependent because science changes, and a view that was once well-supported science may later be rejected or retained only as an approximation.
summaries.why_it_matters: The label affects how we respond to claims. A normal scientific error may be corrected through criticism, while pseudoscientific systems can use evasive strategies that protect them from counterevidence. This distinction matters in medical decisions, environmental policy, courts, journalism, and education. It also encourages intellectual care: criticism should distinguish genuine scientific disagreement from attempts to make unsupported claims appear equally credible.

important_terms.definition: The philosophical task of deciding how science differs from pseudoscience and from other non-scientific activities.
A statement or theory is falsifiable when it could conflict with some possible observation; this was Karl Popper’s proposed scientific criterion.
A continuing set of theories and investigations judged by whether it produces new, confirmed predictions and advances knowledge.
A theory of knowledge that concerns whether beliefs are supported well enough to count as reliable or justified.
The view that science is recognized through a group of overlapping features rather than one feature shared by every scientific practice.

questions_to_think_about: Is falsifiability enough to distinguish science from pseudoscience?
Should a theory be judged alone, or as part of a research community and research programme?
What is the difference between healthy skepticism and denial of well-supported science?
Can a checklist of warning signs avoid becoming too long or too rigid?
Why can experts agree about particular cases while disagreeing about a general definition?

summaries.example: Suppose a social-media account promotes a health product. It uses scientific-looking graphs and invites a few supporters to share success stories. When independent tests do not show the same result, the account blames the testers and points only to positive examples. The question is not merely whether the product’s claim is false. We should also ask whether the promoters are using the appearance of science while avoiding fair tests and criticism.
summaries.summary: The entry examines how to distinguish science from pseudoscience, a problem connected with deciding which beliefs deserve our trust. It warns that “not science,” “unscientific,” and “pseudoscientific” do not mean exactly the same thing. A subject can be outside science without pretending to be science, and a scientist can make an honest error without creating pseudoscience. A commonly discussed definition combines two features: the activity lacks scientific standing, and its main supporters try to make it seem scientific. A broader version focuses on whether a doctrine presents itself as the most reliable knowledge in its area. Philosophers have proposed different criteria, including verifiability, falsifiability, the ability to solve research puzzles, scientific progress, and shared standards of criticism. Since each rule has weaknesses, some proposals use several signs at once. The entry also distinguishes pseudo-theory promotion from science denial and notes that science changes over time. These difficulties do not prevent practical judgments, but they show why the general definition remains philosophically unsettled.
key_ideas: Pseudoscience is narrower than non-science and usually narrower than merely unscientific work.
A single mistake, bad measurement, or failed experiment is normally bad science, not pseudoscience.
Pseudoscience commonly includes a continuing unusual doctrine plus an attempt to look scientific or to claim the authority of science.
Philosophers disagree about the best test: possible disproof, puzzle-solving, progress, openness, or several features together.
Science denial and pseudo-theory promotion are related but different forms of pseudoscience.
There is often agreement about particular examples even though there is no universally accepted definition.
summaries.why_it_matters: Claims presented as science can influence choices about treatment, vaccination, climate policy, education, journalism, and court evidence. Understanding pseudoscience helps people notice selective examples, unrepeatable tests, refusal to consider disconfirming evidence, and fake controversies. At the same time, the topic teaches fairness: not every error or disagreement is pseudoscience, and scientific conclusions can develop as evidence improves.

important_terms.definition: The effort to draw or explain the boundary between science, pseudoscience, and other kinds of belief or knowledge.
A claim is falsifiable if some possible observation could show that it is wrong.
A belief system or theory that its supporters repeatedly promote, especially when it conflicts with accepted scientific knowledge.
The study of what makes beliefs well-supported, reliable, or justified.
A method that uses several signs together instead of relying on one rule to identify pseudoscience.

questions_to_think_about: Why is one failed experiment not automatically pseudoscience?
How can scientific-looking organizations create a false impression of reliability?
What is the difference between questioning evidence and denying evidence?
Would a list of warning signs be more useful than one strict rule?
How might scientific change make classification difficult?
